claim: The NDC80 complex is the major coupler of the kinetochore to microtubules.
source: The highly conserved NDC80 complex is the major coupler of the kinetochore to microtubules (Cheeseman et al., 2006; DeLuca et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cheeseman et al., 2006 and DeLuca et al., 2006

claim: Approximately 240 NDC80 complexes are recruited at the outer layer of each kinetochore in human mitotic cells.
source: In human mitotic cells, ~240 NDC80 complexes are recruited at the outer layer of each kinetochore (Suzuki et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Suzuki et al., 2015

claim: NDC80 complexes interact with approximately 20 kinetochore microtubules by directly binding to them.
source: In human mitotic cells, ~240 NDC80 complexes are recruited at the outer layer of each kinetochore (Suzuki et al., 2015) and interact with ~20 kMTs by directly binding to them (Cheeseman and Desai, 2008; Maiato et al., 2004; Rieder, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cheeseman and Desai, 2008; Maiato et al., 2004; Rieder, 1982

claim: The binding affinity of NDC80 for microtubules decreases upon phosphorylation of the N-terminal tail of Ndc80/Hec1 protein by Aurora B kinase in vitro.
source: In vitro experiments showed that the binding affinity of NDC80 for microtubules decreases upon the phosphorylation of the N-terminal tail of Ndc80/Hec1 protein by Aurora B kinase (Cheeseman et al., 2006; Zaytsev et al., 2014, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to in vitro experiments from Cheeseman et al., 2006; Zaytsev et al., 2014, 2015

claim: The fluorescence decay of mTurquoise2-NDC80 in the absence of FlAsH is well described as a single exponential with a lifetime of 3.75 ± 0.09 ns (SD).
source: We found that their fluorescence decays are well described as a single exponential with a lifetime of 3.75 ± 0.09 ns (SD) (Figure 1C, left, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental FLIM measurements shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A

claim: In the presence of FlAsH labeling, the fluorescence decay of mTurquoise2-NDC80 is well fit by a sum of two exponentials with lifetimes 3.71 ± 0.04 ns (SE) and 0.75 ± 0.12 ns (SE).
source: The fluorescence decay in the presence of FlAsH labeling was well fit by a sum of two exponentials with lifetimes 3.71 ± 0.04 ns (SE) and 0.75 ± 0.12 ns (SE) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental FLIM measurements and fitting shown in Figure 1D

claim: 13 ± 1% (SE) of donor fluorophores are engaged in FRET in the presence of FlAsH labeling.
source: The relative amplitude of the short- and long-lifetime exponentials are 0.13 ± 0.01 (SE) and 0.87 ± 0.01 (SE), respectively, thus 13 ± 1% (SE) of donor fluorophores are engaged in FRET.
evidence: Calculated from the relative amplitudes of the two-exponential fit to FLIM data

claim: Incubating cells with nocodazole to depolymerize microtubules caused a reduction of NDC80 FRET fraction from 13 ± 1% (SE) to 3 ± 1% (SE).
source: Incubating cells with nocodazole to depolymerize microtubules caused a reduction (p<10−10, two-sided Z-test) of NDC80 FRET fraction from 13 ± 1% (SE) to 3 ± 1% (SE) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements after nocodazole treatment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D

claim: The Förster radius between mTurquoise2 and TC-FlAsH is 5.90 ± 0.10 nm (SE).
source: Fitting the decay model to the data estimated the Förster radius to be 5.90 ± 0.10 nm (SE).
evidence: Determined through combination of FLIM measurements and Monte Carlo simulations as described in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: NDC80 more than 8 nm away from the kMT do not contribute to the short-lifetime FRET state.
source: We next performed large-scale Monte Carlo simulations of mTurquoise2-NDC80 at various distances between the calponin homology (CH) domain of Hec1/Ndc80 protein (the NDC80 complex's microtubule binding domain adjacent to mTurquoise2 [Alushin et al., 2010]) and FlAsH-labeled microtubules and simulated the fluorescence decay curves, which revealed that NDC80 more than 8 nm away from the kMT do not contribute to the short-lifetime FRET state (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: Determined by Monte Carlo simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and B

claim: 42% of attached mTurquoise2-NDC80 contribute to the short-lifetime FRET state.
source: We found that the NDC80 FRET fraction increases linearly with the NDC80 binding fraction with a slope of 0.42 ± 0.08, indicating that 42% of attached mTurquoise2-NDC80 contribute to the short-lifetime FRET state (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: Determined by Monte Carlo simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C

claim: The measured FRET fraction of 13% corresponds to 31% of NDC80 complexes being bound to kMTs.
source: Thus, the measured FRET fraction of 13% in Figure 1D corresponds to 31% of NDC80 complexes being bound to kMTs.
evidence: Calculated by dividing the measured FRET fraction by the conversion factor of 0.42

claim: The average NDC80-kMT binding gradually increases as mitosis progresses, with NDC80 FRET fraction rising from 7% in early prometaphase to 14% in late metaphase, and reaching about 18% in anaphase.
source: We found that the average NDC80-kMT binding gradually increases as mitosis progresses, with NDC80 FRET fraction rising from 7% in early prometaphase to 14% in late metaphase, and reaching about 18% in anaphase (corresponding to NDC80 binding fractions of 17% in prometaphase; 33% in late metaphase; and 43% in anaphase) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET measurements shown in Figure 2A

claim: Centered kinetochores exhibit 2.0 ± 0.4 times higher NDC80 binding than off-centered kinetochores.
source: We compared the extent of the NDC80-kMT binding of kinetochores centered at the metaphase plate to those located off-centered (Figure 2B), and found that the centered kinetochores exhibit 2.0 ± 0.4 times higher NDC80 binding than the off-centered kinetochores.
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET measurements comparing centered and off-centered kinetochores shown in Figure 2B

claim: NDC80-kMT binding continuously increases over time for kinetochores located in the center region during prometaphase.
source: NDC80-kMT binding continuously increases over time for the kinetochores located in the center region, but remains constant with the FRET fraction of ~7% for the kinetochores in the off-center region (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by time-course FLIM-FRET measurements shown in Figure 2D

claim: NDC80-kMT binding remains constant with FRET fraction of ~7% for kinetochores in the off-center region during prometaphase.
source: NDC80-kMT binding continuously increases over time for the kinetochores located in the center region, but remains constant with the FRET fraction of ~7% for the kinetochores in the off-center region (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by time-course FLIM-FRET measurements shown in Figure 2D

claim: The NDC80 FRET fraction is higher at trailing kinetochores (12.8 ± 0.5%, SEM) than leading kinetochores (11.4 ± 0.5%, SEM).
source: We found that the NDC80 FRET fraction is higher at trailing kinetochores (12.8 ± 0.5%, SEM) than leading kinetochores (11.4 ± 0.5%, SEM), regardless of their speeds (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET measurements on leading and trailing kinetochores shown in Figure 3C

claim: There is a highly significant positive correlation between NDC80 FRET fraction and K-K distance during chromosome oscillations.
source: We used FLIM-FRET analysis to measure the NDC80 binding in groups of sister kinetochores with similar K-K distances, and observed a highly significant positive correlation (p<0.005) between NDC80 FRET fraction and K-K distance (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET measurements correlated with K-K distance shown in Figure 3D

claim: Taxol treatment greatly reduced K-K distances from 1.19 ± 0.19 μm (untreated) to 0.90 ± 0.10 μm.
source: Thus, in order to investigate a wider range of K-K distance, we treated cells with taxol, a microtubule-stabilizing drug, which greatly reduced K-K distances (0.90 ± 0.10 μm, taxol vs. 1.19 ± 0.19 μm, untreated, SD, p<10−30) (Figure 3E)
evidence: Supported by measurements of K-K distance after taxol treatment shown in Figure 3E

claim: STLC treatment reduced K-K distances to 0.87 ± 0.10 μm.
source: As an alternative way to reduce the tension, we inhibited Eg5 with 5 μM S-trityl-L-cysteine (STLC) (Skoufias et al., 2006). STLC-treated cells form monopolar spindles with reduced K-K distances (0.87 ± 0.10 μm, SD, p<10−30) (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by measurements of K-K distance after STLC treatment shown in Figure 3E

claim: The NDC80 FRET fraction continually increases with K-K distance over the full range of K-K distance when combining data from untreated, taxol-treated and STLC-treated cells.
source: Combining the data of untreated, taxol-treated and STLC-treated (only poleward-facing kinetochores) cells, we found that the NDC80 FRET fraction continually increases with K-K distance over the full range of K-K distance (positive correlation, p<0.00005) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by combined FLIM-FRET measurements across different treatments shown in Figure 3D

claim: Aurora B inhibition by ZM447439 causes a gradual increase in NDC80 FRET fraction over ~10 min, from 9% to nearly 18%.
source: We first added the ATP-competitive Aurora B inhibitor, ZM447439, to late prometaphase cells, and observed a gradual increase in NDC80 FRET fraction over ~10 min, from 9% to nearly 18% (corresponding to 21% NDC80 binding fraction before Aurora B inhibition and 43% after the inhibition) (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by time-course FLIM-FRET measurements after Aurora B inhibition shown in Figure 4A

claim: The NDC80 FRET fraction decreased with the number of phospho-mimicking mutations, from 16.0 ± 0.5% with 9A-Hec1 to 5.8 ± 0.5% with 2D-Hec1 and to 4.8 ± 0.3% with 9D-Hec1.
source: The NDC80 FRET fraction decreased with the number of phospho-mimicking mutations, from 16.0 ± 0.5% with 9A-Hec1 (all nine phosphorylation sites substituted with Ala) to 5.8 ± 0.5% with 2D-Hec1 (two sites, S44 and S55, substituted with Asp while the others with Ala) and to 4.8 ± 0.3% with 9D-Hec1 (all nine sites substituted with Asp) (mean ± SEM, Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET measurements on phosphomimetic mutants shown in Figure 4C

claim: After Aurora B inhibition, the NDC80 FRET fraction in 2D-Hec1-expressing cells increases by only 0.02 ± 0.01 (SE), substantially smaller than the increase observed in cells with endogenous Hec1 (0.09 ± 0.01 (SE)).
source: After the addition of ZM447439, the NDC80 FRET fraction increases by only 0.02 ± 0.01 (SE), which is statistically significant (p<0.001), but substantially smaller than the increase observed in cells with endogenous Hec1 (0.09 ± 0.01 (SE)) (compare Figure 4D–4A).
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET measurements comparing 2D-Hec1 and endogenous Hec1 responses to Aurora B inhibition shown in Figures 4D and 4A

claim: The modulation of NDC80 binding to kMTs by Aurora B predominantly occurs through the phosphorylation of the N-terminal tail of Hec1/Ndc80.
source: Thus, the modulation of NDC80 binding to kMTs by Aurora B predominantly occurs through the phosphorylation of the N-terminal tail of Hec1/Ndc80.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of Aurora B inhibition effects in endogenous Hec1 vs 2D-Hec1 cells

claim: During ZM447439 treatment, the fraction of Aurora B sensors in the non-FRET state decreased from 0.540 ± 0.007 (SEM) to 0.368 ± 0.012 (SEM).
source: During ZM447439 treatment, we found a continual reduction in the fraction of the Aurora B sensors in the non-FRET state, a proxy for Aurora B phosphorylation, from 0.540 ± 0.007 (SEM) to 0.368 ± 0.012 (SEM) (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET measurements of Aurora B sensor shown in Figure 4E

claim: There is a graded dependence of NDC80-kMT binding on phosphorylation.
source: This analysis showed a graded dependence of NDC80-kMT binding on phosphorylation (Figure 4F), which is consistent with the impact of phosphomimetic Hec1 mutants on NDC80 binding (compare Figure 4C and F) and results from previous in vitro assays (Zaytsev et al., 2014, 2015).
evidence: Supported by analysis combining NDC80 binding and Aurora B sensor measurements shown in Figure 4F, and consistent with previous in vitro assays

claim: After replacing endogenous Hec1 with 9A-Hec1, there is no significant correlation between NDC80 FRET fraction and K-K distance.
source: After replacing the endogenous Hec1 protein with 9A-Hec1, which cannot be phosphorylated on the nine mutated target sites, we no longer observed a significant correlation between NDC80 FRET fraction and K-K distance (p=0.20) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET measurements in 9A-Hec1 cells shown in Figure 5A

claim: 9A-Hec1-expressing cells displayed significantly larger K-K distance than unperturbed cells (1.36 ± 0.21 µm vs 1.19 ± 0.19 µm).
source: 9A-Hec1-expressing cells displayed significantly larger K-K distance than unperturbed cells (1.36 ± 0.21 µm, SD, p<10−30) (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by K-K distance measurements in 9A-Hec1 cells shown in Figure 5B

claim: The phosphorylation of the N-terminal tail of Hec1 is responsible for the correlation between NDC80-kMT binding and K-K distance.
source: Since the strong correlation between NDC80 binding and K-K distance (Figure 3D) is eliminated in the non-phosphorylatable Hec1 mutant 9A-Hec1 (Figure 5A), this argues that the phosphorylation of the N-terminal tail of Hec1 is responsible for the correlation between NDC80-kMT binding and K-K distance.
evidence: Inferred from the elimination of correlation in 9A-Hec1 mutant

claim: 5-ITu treatment for over 15 min did not significantly alter the average K-K distance (1.16 μm ± 0.18 μm, 5-ITu vs. 1.19 μm ± 0.19 μm, untreated).
source: Treating cells with 5-ITu for over 15 min did not significantly alter the average K-K distance (1.16 μm ± 0.18 μm, 5-ITu vs. 1.19 μm ± 0.19 μm, untreated, SD)
evidence: Supported by K-K distance measurements after 5-ITu treatment

claim: 5-ITu treatment did not significantly alter the overall average fraction of NDC80 bound to kMTs (FRET fraction, 11.79 ± 0.02% 5-ITu vs. 11.87 ± 0.02%, untreated).
source: Treating cells with 5-ITu for over 15 min did not significantly alter the average K-K distance (1.16 μm ± 0.18 μm, 5-ITu vs. 1.19 μm ± 0.19 μm, untreated, SD) or the overall average fraction of NDC80 bound to kMTs (FRET fraction, 11.79 ± 0.02% 5-ITu vs. 11.87 ± 0.02%, untreated, SEM)
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET measurements after 5-ITu treatment

claim: 5-ITu treatment eliminated the correlation between K-K distance and NDC80-kMT binding.
source: Treating cells with 5-ITu for over 15 min did not significantly alter the average K-K distance (1.16 μm ± 0.18 μm, 5-ITu vs. 1.19 μm ± 0.19 μm, untreated, SD) or the overall average fraction of NDC80 bound to kMTs (FRET fraction, 11.79 ± 0.02% 5-ITu vs. 11.87 ± 0.02%, untreated, SEM), but eliminated the correlation between K-K distance and NDC80-kMT binding (p=0.41, Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET measurements after 5-ITu treatment shown in Figure 5E and F

claim: The Aurora B activity at kinetochores assessed by Nuf2-targeted Aurora B FRET sensor was not changed by 5-ITu treatment.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the Aurora B activity at kinetochores assessed by Nuf2-targeted Aurora B FRET sensor was not changed by 5-ITu treatment (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by Aurora B FRET sensor measurements shown in Figure 5H

claim: When cells treated with 5-ITu were exposed to ZM447439, NDC80-kMT binding increased to NDC80 FRET fraction of 0.17 ± 0.01 (SEM), indistinguishable from the levels in cells not subject to 5-ITu exposed to ZM447439.
source: Furthermore, when cells treated with 5-ITu were exposed to the Aurora B inhibitor ZM447439, NDC80-kMT binding increased (to NDC80 FRET fraction of 0.17 ± 0.01, SEM) and Aurora B activity at kinetochores decreased (to Aurora B FRET sensor non-FRET fraction of 0.55 ± 0.01, SEM), indistinguishable from the levels in cells not subject to 5-ITu exposed to ZM447439 (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET measurements after combined 5-ITu and ZM447439 treatment shown in Figure 5G and H

claim: The intensity of INCENP-mCherry at NDC80 linearly decreases with K-K distance over the full range of K-K distance.
source: Combining the data of untreated and taxol-treated cells, we found that the intensity of INCENP-mCherry at NDC80 linearly decreases with K-K distance over the full range of K-K distance (p<10−6).
evidence: Supported by spinning-disk confocal microscopy measurements of INCENP-mCherry intensity

claim: In the presence of 10 μM 5-ITu, the concentration of Aurora B at NDC80 was greatly reduced and independent of K-K distance.
source: We next investigated how the concentration of Aurora B at the location of NDC80 is influenced by haspin inhibition. In the presence of 10 μM 5-ITu, the concentration of Aurora B at NDC80 was greatly reduced and independent of K-K distance (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by INCENP-mCherry intensity measurements after 5-ITu treatment shown in Figure 6B

claim: The fraction of β-tubulin labeled with TC-FlAsH was estimated to be 26.1 ± 5.4%.
source: CRISPR-mediated endogenous tubulin tagging ensures low cell-to-cell variation and a high fraction of labeled β-tubulin, which was estimated to be 26.1 ± 5.4% (SD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and see Supplemental experiments in Materials and methods).
evidence: Estimated through combination of 3D fluorescence microscopy and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy as described in Supplemental experiments

claim: The tension dependency of NDC80-kMT binding requires phosphorylation of the N-terminal tail of Hec1.
source: We show that this tension dependency requires phosphorylation of the N-terminal tail of Hec1, a component of the NDC80 complex, and the proper localization of Aurora B kinase, which modulates NDC80 binding.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing elimination of tension dependency in 9A-Hec1 mutant

claim: The tension dependency of NDC80-kMT binding requires proper localization of Aurora B kinase.
source: We show that this tension dependency requires phosphorylation of the N-terminal tail of Hec1, a component of the NDC80 complex, and the proper localization of Aurora B kinase, which modulates NDC80 binding.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing elimination of tension dependency after haspin inhibition

claim: NDC80 binding is modulated in a chromosome autonomous fashion over prometaphase and metaphase.
source: We found that NDC80 binding is modulated in a chromosome autonomous fashion over prometaphase and metaphase, and is predominantly regulated by centromere tension.
evidence: Supported by observations of different NDC80 binding in centered vs off-centered kinetochores

claim: NDC80 binding is predominantly regulated by centromere tension.
source: We found that NDC80 binding is modulated in a chromosome autonomous fashion over prometaphase and metaphase, and is predominantly regulated by centromere tension.
evidence: Supported by strong correlation between NDC80 binding and K-K distance (a proxy for tension)

claim: Chromosome segregation errors lead to aneuploidy and micronuclei formation, which are closely associated with cancer, infertility, and birth defects.
source: Chromosome segregation errors lead to aneuploidy and micronuclei formation, which are closely associated with cancer, infertility, and birth defects (Santaguida and Amon, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santaguida and Amon, 2015

claim: Error correction is largely due to the detachment of kinetochore microtubules being regulated by tension across centromeres.
source: Previous works suggested that error correction is largely due to the detachment of kinetochore microtubules (kMTs) being regulated by the tension across centromeres, which selectively destabilizes erroneous kMT attachments bearing low tension and stabilizes proper attachments under high tension (Nicklas and Ward, 1994; Liu et al., 2009; Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Lampson and Cheeseman, 2011; Godek et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies

claim: The rest length of K-K distance in human cells in the absence of microtubules is 0.73 ± 0.04 μm.
source: In the absence of microtubules, the rest length of K-K distance in human cell is 0.73 ± 0.04 μm (Tauchman et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tauchman et al., 2015

claim: Each kMT can be contacted by approximately 40 NDC80 complexes.
source: Furthermore, previous estimates have found that each kMT can be contacted by approximately 40 NDC80 complexes (Zaytsev et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zaytsev et al., 2014

claim: There are on average ~20 kMTs per kinetochore in human cells.
source: As on average there are ~20 kMTs per kinetochore in human cells (Maiato et al., 2004; Rieder, 1982)
evidence: Supported by citations to Maiato et al., 2004 and Rieder, 1982

claim: The percentage of polymerized β-tubulin in a mitotic human tissue culture cell is 36 ± 7%.
source: A previous study (Dumontet et al., 1996) estimated the percentage of polymerized β-tubulin in a mitotic human tissue culture cell to be 36 ± 7%.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dumontet et al., 1996

claim: The total concentration of tubulin dimer in a tissue culture cell is ~ 20 μM.
source: Since the total concentration of tubulin dimer in a tissue culture cell is ~ 20 μM (Hiller and Weber, 1978)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hiller and Weber, 1978

claim: Taxol treatment causes an increase in the number of kMTs.
source: Our results argue that the increase in NDC80 binding with increasing tension is caused by changes in affinity, because: (1) the addition of taxol causes a reduction in tension and a reduction in NDC80 binding (Figure 3D and E), but an increase in the number of kMTs (McEwen et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citation to McEwen et al., 1997

claim: Mutating NDC80 changes the number of kMTs in a manner that argues that increasing NDC80-kMT binding increases the stability of kMTs.
source: Consistent with this, previous work showed that mutating NDC80 changes the number of kMTs in a manner that argues that increasing NDC80-kMT binding increases the stability of kMTs (Guimaraes et al., 2008; Zaytsev et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guimaraes et al., 2008 and Zaytsev et al., 2014

claim: kMT stability increases during mitotic progression.
source: Our work further supports the connection between NDC80-kMT binding and kMT stability by comparing our results with previous measurements of the rate of kMT detachment from kinetochores: NDC80-kMT binding increases during mitotic progression (Figure 2), while kMT stability increases (Zhai et al., 1995; Kabeche and Compton, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhai et al., 1995 and Kabeche and Compton, 2013

claim: Aurora B inhibition causes an increase in kMT stability.
source: NDC80-kMT binding increases in response to Aurora B inhibition (Figure 4), which causes an increase in kMT stability (Cimini et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cimini et al., 2006

claim: Reconstituted kinetochores bind more strongly to polymerizing microtubules than depolymerizing microtubules.
source: NDC80 preferentially binds to polymerizing kMTs over depolymerizing kMTs (Figure 3C), while reconstituted kinetochores bind more strongly to polymerizing microtubules than depolymerizing microtubules (Akiyoshi et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Akiyoshi et al., 2010

claim: The stability of kMTs increases with increasing tension.
source: NDC80-kMT binding increases with increasing tension (Figure 3D), and the stability of kMTs increase with increasing tension (Nicklas and Koch, 1969; Akiyoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nicklas and Koch, 1969 and Akiyoshi et al., 2010

claim: The detachment rate of kMTs from kinetochores is reduced when tension is increased.
source: The detachment rate of kMTs from kinetochores was shown to be reduced when tension was increased using glass needles in classic micromanipulation experiments by Bruce Nicklas (Nicklas and Koch, 1969).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nicklas and Koch, 1969

claim: The differential binding of NDC80 to leading vs trailing kinetochores provides an explanation for the higher detachment rate of depolymerizing microtubules from kinetochores in vitro.
source: This differential binding of NDC80 provides an explanation for the higher detachment rate of depolymerizing microtubules from kinetochores in vitro (Akiyoshi et al., 2010)
evidence: Inferred from the observed preferential binding of NDC80 to trailing (polymerizing) kinetochores, and supported by citation to Akiyoshi et al., 2010

claim: The increased NDC80-kMT binding after Aurora B inhibition may underlie the reduction in detachment of kMTs from kinetochores after Aurora B inhibition observed in photoactivation experiments.
source: The increased NDC80-kMT binding after Aurora B inhibition may underlie the reduction in detachment of kMTs from kinetochores after Aurora B inhibition, observed in photoactivation experiments (Cimini et al., 2006).
evidence: Speculative connection between observed NDC80 binding increase and previous observations, supported by citation to Cimini et al., 2006

claim: The tension dependency of NDC80-kMT interactions arises from the nonlinearity of Aurora B autoactivation and the change in Aurora B concentration at NDC80 with centromere tension.
source: Taking together, this leads to a biophysical model of the tension dependency of NDC80-kMT interactions, which arises from the nonlinearity of Aurora B autoactivation and the change in Aurora B concentration at NDC80 with centromere tension.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from mathematical modeling that integrates multiple experimental observations

claim: The tension dependency of kMT detachment from kinetochores results from the tension dependency of NDC80-kMT binding.
source: Hence, we propose that tension dependency of kMT detachment from kinetochores, which is believed to underlie error correction, results from the tension dependency of NDC80-kMT binding.
evidence: Proposed based on correlations between NDC80 binding and kMT stability across multiple conditions

claim: Error correction ultimately results from the nonlinear autoactivation of Aurora B and the consequent phosphoregulation of NDC80-kMT binding.
source: If correct, this implies that error correction ultimately results from the nonlinear autoactivation of Aurora B and the consequent phosphoregulation of NDC80-kMT binding.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on the proposed model and experimental observations

claim: The temporal increase in NDC80-kMT binding of centered kinetochores is due to the gradual decrease in the number of kinetochores with erroneous attachment that transiently lie on the metaphase plate.
source: We speculate that the temporal increase in NDC80-kMT binding of centered kinetochores is due to the gradual decrease in the number of kinetochores with erroneous attachment that transiently lie on the metaphase plate (Magidson et al., 2011).
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed temporal increase, supported by citation to Magidson et al., 2011

claim: The constant NDC80-kMT binding of off-centered kinetochores argues for a lack of temporal regulation of this subpopulation.
source: The constant NDC80-kMT binding of off-centered kinetochores argues for a lack of temporal regulation of this subpopulation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that off-centered kinetochores maintain constant NDC80 binding over time

claim: The finite concentration of Aurora B at NDC80 after haspin inhibition is the pool of Aurora B that maintains the average level of NDC80-kMT binding.
source: We speculate that the finite concentration of Aurora B at NDC80 after haspin inhibition is the pool of Aurora B that maintains the average level of NDC80-kMT binding as described above.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observation that average NDC80 binding is maintained after haspin inhibition

claim: The observation that inhibiting haspin removes the correlations between NDC80-kMT binding and tension, and between Aurora B localization and tension, but does not affect the distribution of K-K distances, argues that these correlations are caused by the influence of tension on NDC80-kMT binding and Aurora B localization.
source: The observation that inhibiting haspin removes the correlations between NDC80-kMT binding and tension, and between Aurora B localization and tension, but does not affect the distribution of K-K distances, argues that these correlations are caused by the influence of tension on NDC80-kMT binding and Aurora B localization.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of effects observed after haspin inhibition

claim: The observed increase in NDC80 binding over the course of prometaphase to metaphase results from the combination of changes in kMT number and changes in NDC80 binding affinity due to continual increase in tension.
source: We hypothesize that the observed increase in NDC80 binding over the course of prometaphase to metaphase results from the combination of changes in kMT number and the changes in NDC80 binding affinity, due to the continual increase in tension at those times (Magidson et al., 2011).
evidence: Hypothesized explanation combining multiple factors, supported by citation to Magidson et al., 2011

claim: The difference in NDC80 binding between poleward-facing and anti-poleward-facing kinetochores in STLC-treated cells is likely caused by the difference in kMT numbers.
source: The difference in NDC80 binding between poleward-facing and anti-poleward-facing kinetochores in STLC-treated cells is likely caused by the difference in kMT numbers (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from observations in STLC-treated cells shown in supplementary figures

claim: Sister kinetochores with 9A-Hec1 are expected to exhibit the same NDC80 binding affinity.
source: This effect is particularly likely to explain the difference in NDC80 binding between sister kinetochores with 9A-Hec1, since these sister kinetochores are expected to exhibit the same NDC80 binding affinity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Inferred from the fact that 9A-Hec1 cannot be phosphorylated, so both sister kinetochores should have the same affinity

claim: NDC80-kMT binding is a major determinant of the kMT detachment rate.
source: These comparisons argue that the NDC80-kMT binding is a major determinant of the kMT detachment rate.
evidence: Inferred from multiple correlations between NDC80 binding and kMT stability across different conditions

claim: TCSPC FLIM-FRET allows quantitative measurements of the fraction of molecules engaging in FRET, even with spatially varying concentrations of donors and acceptors.
